newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour conference forces vote on pensions.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour conference forces vote on pensions.

text.p: Labour party delegates embarrassed leader Tony Blair on Wednesday by demanding a formal vote on a motion calling for higher state pensions.

Blair and his National Executive Committee (NEC) had recommended that the motion be shelved and that the thorny issue of pensions be referred to a review commission after the forthcoming general election.
The NEC opposed the motion, calling for a restoration of the link between earnings and pensions, on grounds of cost, estimated at 3.5 billion stg.
The result of the vote will not be known until Thursday. Several big unions have backed the NEC's compromise, suggesting Blair will carry the day.
A defeat would show that the left wing of the Labour party still retains the capacity to embarrass its moderate, modernising leaders.

But it would have only symbolic significance because delegates also passed, on a show of hands, an NEC statement recommending that a review commission be set up -- and in the Labour party's rules, NEC policy statements take precedence over conference motions.

The conference was earlier set alight by an impassioned appeal for higher pensions from Baroness Barbara Castle, a veteran former Labour social security secretary, who said the promised review did not go far enough.

Castle, 85, earned a standing ovation after saying present Labour policy to direct aid to the 700,000 poorest pensioners constituted a dangerous attack on the universal welfare state because it would lead to more means testing.

The party's current social security spokeswoman, Harriet Harman, countered that a Labour government would take urgent action to help pensioners but warned that making substanial spending pledges could cost it the next election.
"We owe it to (pensioners) not to make promises we know we can't keep and that we know could threaten our chance to help them in government," Harman said.

"As we found out and as the country found out to its cost in 1983, 1987 and 1992 all the promises in the world will be worth nothing if we lack the discipline on spending that threatens our chances at the election," she added.
